tier_reason: pgtpc (sysbench/ref-mysql.md, sysbench/aws.c5d.metal.extreme.md) lists the PostgreSQL configs and sysbench commands but no compiler, flags or CPU model, and the MySQL 8.0 column is copied from dimitrik.free.fr blog posts run by Oracle's MySQL performance team on a different 48-core 2.7 GHz Optane machine, so it is an unreproducible cross-machine comparison by a single PostgreSQL advocate (42-star repo, no licence): tier C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Queries per second, pgtpc Compare table (sysbench/ref-mysql.md), column 'PGSQL.48C' vs 'MySQL.48C': oltp_point_select 1,814,404 vs 1,050,000 (1.73x, derived from page data); oltp_read_only 941,694 vs 920,000 (1.02x, derived from page data); oltp_update_non_index 269,233 vs 240,000 (1.12x, derived from page data); oltp_read_write 722,907 vs 900,000 (MySQL 1.25x faster, derived from page data). Thread counts per the same pages: the raw point-select table lists 1,814,404 at 64 client threads, and at 48 client threads PostgreSQL did 1,503,656 (1.43x MySQL's published peak, derived from page data); the 'PGSQL.96C' figures are 2,332,928 point-select QPS at 104 client threads (2.22x, derived from page data) and 910,554 read_write QPS at 128 threads (about parity with MySQL's 900,000). The extreme page itself notes MySQL read_write as '39k/78W' (780,000 QPS), inconsistent with the 900,000 in the Compare table. Repo summary: 'PGSQL has a similar write performance and significantly better read performance to MySQL.'
corrections.workload: sysbench oltp_point_select on 8 tables x 50M rows and oltp_read_only, oltp_read_write and oltp_update_non_index on 8 tables x 10M rows, 300 s runs at 1 to 512 threads over a Unix socket, PostgreSQL 14.5 (version stated on the NORMAL-config page) with a 'NOT FOR PRODUCTION' config (fsync off, synchronous_commit off, full_page_writes off, wal_level minimal, autovacuum off, shared_buffers 128GB, tables rebuilt at fillfactor 75 and pg_prewarm'ed) on an AWS c5d.metal, versus MySQL 8.0 peak numbers copied from dimitrik.free.fr blog posts (48 cores with HT, checksum, doublewrite, binlog, PFS and fsync off, latin1).
corrections.caveats: The head-to-head is not same-machine: the PostgreSQL rows were run by the pgtpc author (Vonng) on c5d.metal (PostgreSQL 14.5, listed as 96C 3.6 GHz), while the MySQL 8.0 rows are copied from two dimitrik.free.fr blog posts by Oracle's MySQL performance team (linked from sysbench/ref-mysql.md; the blog and mysql.com are blocked from this session) on a 48-core 2.7 GHz box with 2x Optane P4800X, so clock speed, storage and run conditions differ. Both sides use durability-off 'extreme' settings (pgtpc says MySQL's run turns off checksum, doublewrite, binlog, PFS and fsync and uses latin1; PostgreSQL has fsync, synchronous_commit, full_page_writes and autovacuum off) and are not production configurations. Column labels are loose: 'PGSQL.48C' (comment 'FORCE c=48') holds a point-select figure that the page's own raw data puts at 64 client threads (48 threads gives 1,503,656, 1.43x), and the 96C figures are peaks at 104 and 128 threads. MySQL wins oltp_read_write at 48 threads and only ties at 128, read_only is parity, and the extreme page quotes MySQL read_write as 780,000 in one place and 900,000 in another, so the win is limited to point selects and a small update margin. No compiler, flags or CPU model, so not tier A; the benchmark repo has 42 stars, 20 commits, no LICENSE file and its last commit is 2022-08-22; its author maintains a PostgreSQL distribution and calls MySQL's published benchmark 'shameless'. Category mismatch: PostgreSQL is a client-server RDBMS, not an embedded key-value store, and MySQL is not one of the category's baselines (RocksDB, LevelDB, LMDB, SQLite); no PostgreSQL vs SQLite number was found. Corroboration, same direction: a HammerDB TPROC-C discussion on a laptop (https://github.com/TPC-Council/HammerDB/discussions/259; i7-1165G7, 16 GB, Docker 'latest' images limited to 12 GB, 100 warehouses, 1 virtual user) reports about 14,000 NOPM for PostgreSQL vs about 3,800 for MySQL, with the HammerDB maintainer replying that PostgreSQL performs better on this single-threaded test but that the gap is closer on servers; database versions are not stated. A small Takeruso/rdbms-performance-comparison repo (sysbench 10 threads, 60 s, Docker on WSL) shows near parity in transactions (about 20,963 PostgreSQL vs 20,845 MySQL) with PostgreSQL at 4.77 ms vs 28.78 ms average latency (not re-opened by the verifier). A DoltHub 2024 blog post (Postgres 15.5 vs MySQL 8.0.35) was seen only as a WebSearch summary.

notes: Numbers match the pgtpc pages, but the '48 threads' label is wrong for point select (raw data puts 1,814,404 at 64 threads; 48 threads gives 1.43x) and the 96-thread figures are really 104/128-thread peaks; the MySQL column is copied from Oracle-team blog runs on different hardware, and the page contradicts itself on MySQL read_write (780,000 vs 900,000). Shortcomings to record: cross-machine copied baseline, durability-off configs, MySQL faster or tied on read_write, wrong category (client-server RDBMS in embedded-kv; MySQL not a category baseline), benchmark repo unlicensed and stale; consider a category override or keep-and-document.

tier_reason: First-party Restream benchmark with public Go harness (reindexer-benchmarks: bench_queries_test.go, bench_text_test.go, repo/*.go, run_benches.sh, Dockerfile) and Go 1.9.3 / clang-802.0.42 named, but no optimisation flags for the Mac build and no exact CPU SKU, and the SQLite baseline is misconfigured; tier C.

corrections.baseline: SQLite 3.17.0 via mattn/go-sqlite3 and sqlx, opened with DSN '/tmp/foo.db?mode=memory&cache=shared' (no 'file:' prefix, so go-sqlite3 drops the query string and SQLite runs as an on-disk /tmp/foo.db with default settings, not in memory), with indexes on name and year and an FTS5 table; also compared with Redis, Tarantool, MySQL, MongoDB, Elasticsearch, Sphinx, ArangoDB, RethinkDB and (web only) ClickHouse
corrections.claimed_speedup: Single core get by ID 4,224 ns/op versus SQLite 23,735 (5.6x, derived from page data) and Redis 47,492 (11.2x, derived from page data); 1 condition 17,403 versus SQLite 60,749 (3.5x, derived from page data) and Redis 126,484 (7.3x, derived from page data); 2 conditions 22,531 versus SQLite 61,354 (2.7x, derived from page data); full-text exact 39,722 versus SQLite 1,274,902 (32x, derived from page data) and MySQL 294,697 (7.4x, derived from page data). Web, 8 cores, embedded mode: by ID 158,797 RPS versus SQLite 28,496 (5.6x, derived from page data) and Redis 79,411 (2.0x, derived from page data); 1 filter 70,149 versus SQLite 21,796 (3.2x, derived from page data). Update 27,000 versus SQLite 452 RPS is not like for like (on-disk SQLite with its default synced rollback journal versus in-memory Reindexer), and Redis (30,025) and Tarantool (33,905) beat Reindexer on update.
corrections.caveats: First-party benchmark (Restream) on one 2016 laptop with 2018-era versions (Go 1.9.3, Tarantool 1.7.6.12, Elasticsearch 5.4.3, SQLite 3.17.0, MongoDB 3.4.5); optimisation flags and exact CPU SKU not stated, so tier C rather than A. SQLite baseline misconfigured: repo/sqlite.go opens '/tmp/foo.db?mode=memory&cache=shared' without the 'file:' prefix, and go-sqlite3 (v1.6.0 sqlite3.go Open) strips the query string in that case, so SQLite ran as an on-disk file with the default rollback journal and synchronous=FULL rather than in memory; this mostly inflates the update row (27,000 vs 452 RPS) and adds syscall cost to reads. The Dockerfile used for the web runs installs Go 1.9.2, Elasticsearch 6.x and MongoDB 3.6, not the versions the README lists, and builds Reindexer with make EXTRA_CFLAGS=-DNDEBUG; wrk results are the best of ten 2-second runs per cell (run_benches.sh). The current harness code (go-redis with context API) postdates the published numbers, and the benchmark repo has 2 commits and 1 star. The README labels Redis '2.3.9', which looks like a client or typo rather than a server release; Redis is reached over TCP on 127.0.0.1:6379 through go-redis while Reindexer and SQLite run in-process, so the Redis and other server rows include a network round trip. Redis 1-condition query is a ZRANGEBYSCORE on a sorted set of JSON blobs and Redis has no 2-condition or full-text row. Reindexer is not fastest on update in the web table: Redis 30,025 RPS and Tarantool 33,905 RPS beat embedded Reindexer 27,000. 'Object cache' rows (2,530 ns/op) skip unmarshalling in the other databases, so are not like for like. The benchmark repo imports an internal module path (git.restream.ru/itv-backend/reindexer) instead of the public GitHub path. Reindexer main README claims only 'on par with a typical key-value database' and up to 500K by-id queries/sec per core. Initial category guess was caches; moved to embedded-kv because the benchmark's closest like-for-like baseline is in-process SQLite.

notes: All quoted numbers are on the reindexer-benchmarks readme; metadata confirmed (Apache-2.0, 812 stars, last commit 2026-09-26 'Update to version v5.17.0'). Shortcoming to record: the SQLite baseline described as in-memory actually ran on disk because go-sqlite3 ignores 'mode=memory&cache=shared' without a 'file:' prefix (update row 60x is a durability artifact), plus 2018-era versions, Docker versions differing from README, and Redis/Tarantool faster on update.

Last code commit is 2019-01-25; the 2025-02-13 and 2026-03-03 commits are README edits, and the README says the project is no longer developed, so maintenance is recorded as abandoned. notes: Real, notable (1.9k stars) storage engine, but the only numbers are a 2013 third-hand quote of a dead project page seen through WebSearch snippets, so tier D (downgrade from C). Shortcomings to record: no reachable benchmark, numbers unreproduced by the poster, smaller gap to HyperLevelDB, project no longer developed (last code commit 2019-01-25).
